Urogenital atrophy

Crucially, urinalysis results are *pending and unavailable*, meaning infection (e.g., asymptomatic bacteriuria or low-grade cystitis), microscopic hematuria, or glucosuria have not been ruled out. While urogenital atrophy is a leading non-infectious consideration, diagnosing it *requires supportive evidence*: either clinical exam findings *or* corroborating history (e.g., confirmed menopause, vaginal dryness/pruritus, dyspareunia — none of which are documented). Isolated frequency alone is nonspecific and insufficient for definitive diagnosis. With turns exhausted (10/10), no further data can be gathered; thus, the diagnosis cannot be confirmed with current evidence.

[FEEDBACK] Diagnosis of urogenital atrophy requires either (1) documented menopausal status + characteristic vaginal exam findings (e.g., pale, thin, friable epithelium), or (2) supportive symptoms (e.g., vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, pruritus) — none of which are reported.
